concepts.def: Main melodic theme of a jazz performance, played at the start and end, with improvisations on its chord changes between.
Chord progression of a tune, which improvisers outline melodically through chord-tone and scale choices.
Style based on scales rather than chord changes, pioneered by Miles Davis on 'Kind of Blue' (1959).
Fast, virtuosic 1940s style developed by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, featuring complex harmony and rapid eighth-note lines.
Unequal subdivision of beats where eighth notes are performed with a long-short feel, fundamental to mainstream jazz.
Improvised chordal accompaniment provided by piano or guitar behind a soloist, supporting and responding to the improvisation.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Area of Study 5: Jazz — a core area of A-Level Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area of Study 5: Jazz brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area of Study 5: Jazz.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which Miles Davis album popularised modal jazz?
options: Bitches Brew
Kind of Blue
Sketches of Spain
Birth of the Cool

mcqs.q: Which saxophonist is most associated with the development of bebop?

Charlie Parker
Stan Getz
Ornette Coleman

mcqs.q: What is the function of the bridge in a pop song?
options: It is the same as the chorus.
Three notes played at once.
It is the very first section.
To provide contrast before the final chorus, often by changing melody, key, or texture.

mcqs.q: What does 'piano' (p) mean as a dynamic marking?
options: Quiet/soft.
Slow.
The instrument piano.
Three notes played at once.
Vibrato on a single note.
Three notes played at once.
It is the very first section.
Rapid alternation between the written note and the note a step above.
